content: Milk of Magnesia is an aqueous suspension of magnesium hydroxide (Mg(OH)₂) in water. It functions as a saline osmotic laxative, which means it draws water into the intestines to promote bowel movements. The name Milk of Magnesia originates from its milky white appearance and the magnesium content in its composition. The term Milk of Magnesia was first used in 1880 by Charles Henry Phillips, who formulated a mildly alkaline suspension of magnesium hydroxide at a concentration of approximately 8% weight/volume. This product was sold under the brand name Phillips' Milk of Magnesia for medicinal purposes. While the name may have been associated with GlaxoSmithKline at some point, trademark registrations indicate that Milk of Magnesia is currently registered to Bayer, and Phillips' Milk of Magnesia is registered to Sterling Drug. In the United Kingdom, the generic name for these products is Cream of Magnesia or Magnesium Hydroxide Mixture, BP. Milk of Magnesia is available over-the-counter in various forms, including chewable tablets, capsules, and liquids, often in different flavors. Physicians recommend taking it with a full glass of water or juice to aid absorption. However, it may interact with antibiotics, and individuals who are pregnant or nursing should consult a physician before use. Its primary use is to relieve constipation, but it is also effective for indigestion and heartburn. When taken orally as a laxative, the osmotic action of magnesium hydroxide draws fluids into the intestines, distending the bowel and stimulating nerves in the colon wall. This induces peristalsis, leading to the evacuation of colonic contents. Historically, it was marketed with the slogan, Take MOM in the PM, for BM in the AM. It is also used as an antacid, though modern formulations often combine it with aluminum hydroxide to counteract unwanted laxative effects. According to the MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, Milk of Magnesia can be applied topically to treat canker sores (aphthous ulcers). It is also used as a folk remedy for seborrhea and dandruff when massaged into the scalp before washing or shampooing. However, the mechanism behind its effectiveness in these applications remains unclear. When ingested, Milk of Magnesia enters the stomach, where it can act in one of two ways depending on the dose. At lower doses (around 5 grams in adults), it neutralizes stomach acid by combining hydroxide ions from Mg(OH)₂ with hydrogen ions (H⁺) from gastric hydrochloric acid. As a laxative, it is typically dosed at 2–5 grams. Magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) are poorly absorbed in the intestines, so they draw water into the intestinal lumen via osmosis. This increased water content softens the stool and increases its volume, which naturally stimulates intestinal motility. Additionally, magnesium ions may trigger the release of cholecystokinin (CCK), which further promotes water and electrolyte accumulation in the intestines and enhances motility. Non-basic magnesium solutions, such as magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄), are equally effective as laxatives on a molar basis. Caution is advised when using Milk of Magnesia, as excessive use can lead to diarrhea. Only a small amount of magnesium is typically absorbed from the intestines unless the individual has a magnesium deficiency. Magnesium is primarily excreted by the kidneys, so long-term daily use of Milk of Magnesia in individuals with renal failure could theoretically result in hypermagnesemia (elevated magnesium levels in the blood). Adverse reactions to Milk of Magnesia may include weakness, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with higher doses increasing the likelihood of these effects. Patients with severe chronic kidney disease are advised to avoid overconsumption, as impaired kidney function can lead to toxic magnesium levels in the blood. Healthy individuals should not use this medication continuously for more than one week, as prolonged use may result in excessively harsh laxative effects.
